Kulintang 源自東南亞古老鑼樂傳統，早期可能用於信號，後吸收爪哇巽他人的: The kulintang comes from an old gong tradition in Southeast Asia; at first it may have served for signalling, and it developed later by taking in the bossed gongs of the Javanese Sundanese. Two routes of spread have been proposed: one through Bandar Masin, Brunei and the Sulu archipelago, the other through Timor, Sulawesi and the Moluccas to Mindanao. European explorers left the earliest record in the sixteenth century; in Borneo it was first used for harvest festivals and at the Brunei court, and later, as empires expanded, it entered the rituals of the inland Dayak peoples. In 1968 José Maceda and Aga Mayo Butocan promoted notation and improvisation at the University of the Philippines, which brought the tradition back into notice.
Kulintang以橫置小鑼奏旋律，配大鑼與鼓，見於菲律賓南部、馬來西亞東部、印: The kulintang plays melody on a row of small gongs laid horizontally, with large gongs and drums, and it is found in the southern Philippines, eastern Malaysia, eastern Indonesia, Brunei and Timor. Traditionally it is used for harvest festivals, at the Brunei court, in tribal ritual, and before and after war parties and on martial occasions; the Magindanao ensemble of five or six instruments is called the basalen or palabunibunyan. It also appears in the totoobuan ensemble of Buru Island.

Its melodic range comes from this row of metal gongs, based on a pentatonic scale, with larger hanging gongs and drums accompanying. Compared with the gamelan, which belongs to the same Southeast Asian gong-chime culture, the gamelan mostly builds melody within a skeleton and fixed entry intervals, while the kulintang's framework is looser, with no fixed time intervals, and improvisation is more common. The kulintang is an idiophone of the Southeast Asian gong-chime culture, made of a row of small metal pot gongs laid horizontally on a wooden frame, struck on the boss with two wooden mallets, and accompanied by larger hanging gongs and drums. Its melody is mostly pentatonic, and it is common in the southern Philippines, eastern Malaysia, eastern Indonesia, Brunei and Timor. It comes from a local signalling tradition and later took in the bossed gongs of the Javanese Sundanese; in Borneo it was used for harvest rites and at the Brunei court, and it also appears in tribal ritual, before and after head-hunting, and on Malay martial occasions.
kulintang的發聲體為金屬製的凸心鑼，來源稱其為金屬鑼鍋，橫置於架上；另有: The sounding bodies of the kulintang are bossed metal gongs, which the source calls metal gong pots, laid horizontally on a frame; there are also larger hanging gongs and drums. They are struck on the boss with two wooden mallets. Some ensembles also use a set of bronze gongs and a single gong. As for the frame, the drum bodies, the drumheads and the other parts, the source does not state their materials.

演奏時將一組小鑼橫置於架上，以兩根木槌敲擊鑼面凸起發聲。初學先熟悉五聲音階與合奏: Set the row of small gongs horizontally on the frame and strike the bosses with two wooden mallets. A beginner first gets to know the pentatonic scale and the layered rhythmic parts of the ensemble, then practises improvising. Aga Mayo Butocan's notation and the Palabunibunyan repertory collection are useful references, starting from the basic stroke and the fit with the accompaniment.
